title: A Aftermath for the Wardrobe
premise: Cyrus Okonkwo, once the conservatory's most celebrated piano prodigy, returns twenty years later not to perform but to mop its floors, hiding a ruined hand and an inventory of unsaid things. At his mother's funeral, a stranger named Vera addresses the family by 'Nwachukwu' — a name buried with the father Cyrus never speaks of — and reveals she holds letters proving Cyrus's father did not abandon them but was erased. As Cyrus and his sister Adaeze trace the name through conservatory archives and family silence, they discover their mother traded the truth of their father's disappearance for the patronage that funded Cyrus's career: his gift was bought with a lie. In the final chapters, Cyrus must choose between protecting the myth that made him and claiming the erased man whose name might finally let him play again.
about_author: Xanthe Pemberton is the pen name of a former conservatory librarian who spent a decade cataloguing other people's unfinished symphonies before writing her own. She lives near a defunct music school and keeps, like her characters, a careful inventory of everything unsaid.

chapters.title: The Inventory
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. Twenty years after his debut, Cyrus pushes a janitor's cart through the conservatory where he once performed, cataloguing in a notebook everything he cannot say aloud — including his mangled left hand. When news of his mother's death arrives over the intercom, he finishes mopping the recital hall first. Emotional beat: grief deferred into ritual.

chapters.title: A Name Nobody Uses
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. At the funeral, amid rehearsed condolences, a composed stranger named Vera approaches the family and calls them by 'Nwachukwu,' a surname that makes Adaeze flinch and their uncle go silent. She leaves only a card and the words 'your father wrote.' Emotional beat: a crack opens in the family's polished surface.

chapters.title: What the House Keeps
chapters.summary: Adaeze's POV. Sorting their mother's belongings, Adaeze finds a locked cedar wardrobe that predates Cyrus's birth, keyless, which their mother forbade anyone to open even in illness. She notices the funeral photographs have one figure cropped out. Emotional beat: suspicion curdling into resolve.

chapters.title: The Patron
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. Cyrus visits Sir Edmund Hale, the aging patron who funded his career, expecting comfort; instead Hale is evasive about 1987 and lets slip that Cyrus's scholarship was 'settled as a kindness, not earned.' Cyrus plays nothing on the lobby piano, unable to bear the sound. Emotional beat: the myth begins to smell of transaction.

chapters.title: Vera's Letters
chapters.summary: Vera's POV (first departure). Vera, the daughter of the father's business partner, reveals she has held letters for decades — her father's dying request — proving Nwachukwu Okonkwo didn't flee debts but was driven out after refusing to falsify conservatory accounts. She wants the family's blessing to publish, or she'll publish anyway. Emotional beat: truth as inheritance, unwelcome.

chapters.title: The Wardrobe Opens
chapters.summary: Adaeze's POV. Adaeze forces the wardrobe and finds her father's belongings: a violin, unopened letters addressed to Cyrus at age ten, and a ledger showing payments from Hale to their mother spanning Cyrus's entire education. The price of survival, itemized. Emotional beat: betrayal and terrible clarity.

chapters.title: Concerto for One Hand
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. Confronted by Adaeze, Cyrus denies it violently — the lie is load-bearing; without the noble-mother narrative, his sacrifice means nothing. He nearly burns the letters but instead reads one, hearing his father's voice for the first time since childhood. Emotional beat: rage breaking against longing.

chapters.title: Hale's Reckoning
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. Cyrus confronts Hale with the ledger; the old man confesses without apology — the conservatory needed a scapegoat, and a dead man's reputation was cheap currency for a prodigy's future. He offers Cyrus silence in exchange for burying Vera's publication. Emotional beat: the climax of moral pressure.

chapters.title: The Question They Arranged Around
chapters.summary: Adaeze and Cyrus, alternating. The siblings finally ask what the whole family arranged itself around: who were we protecting, and from what? Their uncle admits he helped crop the photographs. Cyrus chooses to authorize Vera's publication, surrendering the myth that made him. Emotional beat: costly consent.

chapters.title: Everything Said
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. At a small memorial concert, Cyrus performs a piece written for one hand — his own composition, titled 'Nwachukwu' — publicly reclaiming the erased name while accepting the hand that can no longer do what it once could. The inventory notebook closes with a single entry: everything said. Emotional beat: survival re-priced, identity inherited whole.
